THE 1925 CONVENTION

Everyone who attended the annual convention this year has voiced the
opinion that it was certainly the best one he ever attended, and there
were many
present who have enjoyed a number of conventions in the past.
In this, the 92nd year of the fraternity, the Pi chapter were the hosts
on May 7, 8 and 9, and with a full representation of the chapter roll the
opening session was called to order by the President of the Executive
Council, Earl D. Babst, Iota-Phi '93. This convention was the first one
held since Brother Babst became President of the fraternity and he was
warmly received. It was soon discovered that his very presence radiated
his truly great devotion to the ideals of Psi Upsilon, and while all this was
not new to those who have worked with him, yet it was the first real

opportunity for many of the delegates to meet him. We will let them
sing his praises but the enthusiasm was at a high pitch from the opening
of the first session until the Shrine Song had been simg for the last time.

One feature of this year's convention was that all the official delegates
from the chapters lived at the home of the Pi chapter, and thus they
enjoyed a continuous association that proved to be very valuable. No
doubt the custom will prevail at all future conventions. There were many
brothers in attendance from the nearby chapters, who together with the
alumni present made a large gathering that was most enjoyable.

For many years the world in general and particularly the newspapers
have always referred to fraternity conventions as a continuous drinking
bout, but we are more than pleased to record the 1925 convention as one
where the conduct of the delegates was beyond reproach, and in full accord
with the expressed desire of the fraternity. Never was there gathered
together a finer lot of young men, intent on the business before them. They
all had a royal time and the benefits from this convention will surely
accrue for many years to come.

After the first business session the hosts provided an informal Tea
Dance and Buffet Supper. The famous "Isle of Blue Orchestra" from
Colgate furnished the music. As guests of the chapter there were present
about seventy very charming young ladies, many of whom were coeds
from the University, and others were from prominent families of Syracuse.

The gathering broke up about midnight and everyone voted the entire
day and evening a great success.
After the business session on Friday morning, luncheon was again
served at the chapter house and the representatives from the three petition
ing societies were invited to attend as guests so that they might meet all
in attendance at the convention. There were present members from the
Pi UpsilonSociety, of the University of Kansas, from the Wranglers of
Northwestern University, and from Epsilon Phi of McGill University.
After luncheon the convention picture was taken and then followed the
meeting of the Committee of the Whole in one of the buildings of the
University at which time the petitioners were formally presented and
given an opportunity to present their petitions in person. In due course
the convention resumed its regular sessions and later adjourned sine die.
Before adjourning it was voted to hold another meeting of the Committee
of the Whole the following morning in order to allow a "round table dis
cussion" of many interesting subjects that would not come up in convention.
Thus the official business of the convention was completed in three sessions
which were rich in accomplishments, and most pleasing in character.
The convention banquet was held on the evening of the second day,
in the ball room of the Onondaga Hotel. There were over two hundred
present and the singing was broadcasted as well as some of the speeches.
The singing, ably lead by Brother W. F. Merrill, Gamma '99 will long be
remembered.

Dear Brother Barber:
I deeply regret that reasons, over which I have no control, prevent
me from accepting the invitation of your committee to be present at
the Convention of my college fraternity, which is to meet at Syracuse
early in May. It would be a great privilege for me to be there and to
renew the bonds of brotherhood with those whose presence bears witness

to their devotion to Psi Upsilon and to the ideals which have inspired
its members and kept it a vital force for good in the universities and
colleges which are fortunate enough to have chapters of the fraternity.
The spirit of Psi Upsilon is an influence which continues long after
college days are passed, long after the day when parting from his brothers
of the clasped hands a man goes forth to find the place in the world to
which his destiny calls him. It is that fine spirit of comradeship, of con
fidence, of generous helpfulness, acquired, perhaps unconsciously, while he

No brother in Psi Upsilon feels a greater pride than I do in its long

Our toastmaster first introduced Brother Shuart who made a very
inspiring address on the early days on the Pi, reviewing the lives of his
fellow Founders of the chapter. He closed by saying that he had had
such a good time at the convention that he thought he had better return
to Springfield, Mass. and close up his business as in the future he wanted
to be free to attend all the Psi Upsilon conventions. He said the favorite
games played in '75 were "euchre, old maid and others the faculty did
not approve of," and, that while football was not played, that a game was
based on "old cat," played in his day. He said he umpired the first
baseball game between Syracuse and Cornell, and he expressed hope there
will be a revival of athletic relations between the universities.

He paid a tribute to the other founders of Pi chapter, particularly
the late James M. Gilbert of Syracuse, and declared the spirit of Psi U

On February 14 the new
permanent home of the Theta Theta at

marked by the largest gathering of Northwest brothers recorded since

Eighty-one alumni, representing
twelve chapters, and thirty-one members of the active Theta Theta were
present. In addition, the annual initiation was held in the new Chapter
hall, with Brother Charles T. Donworth, Beta, '14, delivering the address.
Brother Charles Paul, Beta, was master of ceremonies.

The architecture of the new house is reminiscent of the English
Tudor period, following a manor type of the same general style of which
the new University of Washington represent an institutional type. The
decorative details, arches, fireplaces, interior and exterior paneling and
beams are designed in the Tudor manner. Features of the exterior are
tall chimneys and steep roofs, with sharply pointed gables. The frontage
of the house is toward the south, and on that .side is a partly open and
partly covered terrace. The construction is brick and tile, with an exterior
finish of stuQco.

The main floor contains the living rooms and dining room, kitchen
and servants' quarters. The second floor has ten study rooms, the library
and a guest suite, while the third story contains the dormitories. Chapter
hall, and an eleventh study. There are fireplaces in the living room, dining
room and library. The basement contains a combined trophy and bUliard
room, and furnace and storage rooms. An oil burning furnace provides
the heat. Hot water is furnished by an automatic heater, while electricity
is used for culinary purposes.

Decorative features include conventional designs of owls, the diamond
and the Roman fasces in central windows of the living room and dining
room, and the coat-of-arms of the Theta Theta in a large ornamental win
dow over the main staircase. The entrance hall is richly paneled and
beamed.

Many of the furnishings were generous gifts of alumni and under
graduate brothers, while draperies for the entire house, which contains
nearly eighty windows, were given by the Chapter Mothers' Club.
The house was financed through the leadership and generosity of
alumni brothers of the Pacific Northwest, both of the Theta Theta and
other chapters, constituting the members of the Lyman Maass Associa
tion of Psi Upsilon, and the Puget Sound Alumni Association. Through
their untiring zeal, the Theta Theta now possesses a home which is
unequaled by any fraternity house at the University of Washington.

WORTHY OF REFLECTION

Ex-Secretary of State Chas. E. Hughes, in a talk some time ago, under
the subject of "A Balanced Life," said as follows:
"What does the Christian character or a balanced hfe mean? It is
this:
"Faith without credulity, conviction without bigotry, charity without
condescension, courage without pugnacity, self-respect without vanity,
humility without obsequiousness, love of humanity without sentimentaUty,
and meekness with power.
"That is our ideal."
I believe you will agree that the expressions present a wonderful
picture of well-balanced character.
We get in the old fable of the hare and the tortoise a graphic illus
tration of lack of balance in one department.
We have among our acquaintances, in and out of our own immediate
environment, men and women who in their particular line have the
qualities of the self-sufficient, self-assertive, and altogether undependable
hare of the fable. We see these quaUties in salesmen, in department heads,
and all the way down the line in our clerical and factory forces. People
who can win races, but who fail at the end of the long pull because, like
the hare, they over-emphasize their ability to think and act quickly, and
under-emphasize that greater characteristic of continually "keeping at it."
We know also among our acquaintances and associates those who par
take more or less of the characteristics of the tortoise, not rapid, in no
wise dynamic, but who are always "at it" and, while their more brilliant
brothers slumber, are pegging along.
In making this comparison we must remember, also, of course, that
not all those who are slower in thought are continually "pegging." The
greatest misfit of all, naturally, is one who possesses neither of the two
endowments, lacking even the virtue of "sticking to it."
The danger of those having more plentiful mental and physical
endowment lies in the tendency to "back and fill" ^to spurt and then hold

back.
Those less plentifully endowed must remember that the tortoise only
can beat the hare when the latter goes to sleep.

Now let us get back to what Secretary Hughes said. He pointed out
eight balances of character.
Faith without credulity 

^Whereas "faith is the essence of things not
seen" it is very different from credulity. A credulous person believes most
anything he hears, and consequently either builds up a wrong faith or
destroys a good faith. One who believes or at least listens to everything
he hears, without a proper capacity to analyze and separate the false from
the true, quite as often loses faith in that in which he should have faith, as
he gets faith in that which he should question. His opinions are unreliable,
and he is not to be depended upon.

229

Conviction without bigotry implies faith in one's own carefully
thought-out ideas, but makes due allowance for the carefully thoughtout
opinions of others.
A bigot insists that what he believes contains the only possible right,
and impudently assumes that which is the prerogative of Divinity, which
alone has a right, because it alone has a knowledge of all facts and condi
tions, to define what is absolutely true.
Charity without Condescencion hits at a lack of balance quite often
observed.
A great many who do a charitable thing for others have a tendency
to feel that they have in part a claim on those whom they have benefited.
A good many people engage in acts of charity that they may "cash
in" when occasion arises.
True charity is forcibly explained in the Bible by this expression:
"When thou givest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right doeth."
True charity means a giving of one's resources or oneself without any
consideration of remuneration whatsoever, implying a love of being helpful
for helpfulness' sake.
Courage without pugnacity is a balance a great many do not possess.
Bluster, bluff, vociferous talking and boastfulness are not characteristics
of true courage.
A bully is never a
courageous hero. Courage is generally expressed
in silent deeds, and perhaps as much in capacity to endure without com
plaint as in the capacity to do and to dare.
Pugnacity is obstreperous bluster, generally discovered by all others
save the possessor of such
qualities.
Self-respect without vanity gives an interesting contrast. Conceit,
false pride, vainglorying are indulged in by the lesser folk as substitutes
for self-respect, most generally through gross ignorance and mental undevelopment. He who thinks to advertise his self-respect by strutting is
woefully out of balance.
Humility without obsequiousness is a lack of balance less often en
countered than others that are mentioned.
Obsequiousness generally appears in the habit of toadying or boot
licking and in seeking favor bj "Kow-towing" to those in a position to
bestow favor.
Humility as a rule represents appreciation of the littleness of the
individual when compared with the
enormity of the Universe and the
Powers above us.
The contrast mentioned, I think, is intended to convey politeness
without assuming the manner of a slave.
Love of humanity without
sentimentality suggests a lack of balance
quite frequently observed, chiefly by those who think an indulgence of
emotion without
corresponding action, represents real love of humanity.
The arousing of one's sentiments is
dissipating and enervating unless
the emotion bears fruit in some act of work.

Unless we execute deeds of service and of self-sacrifice, the expression
of one's love for humanity is sentimentality and that is "bosh."

Meekness with Power is the crux of the whole philosophy of life.
Otherwise we would not have the beatitude "Blessed are the meek
for they shall inherit the earth."
That surely designates that in meekness there is power. In power
without meekness one can have but little influence because meekness de
notes a trueappreciation of one's real position in the scheme of things,
and his dependence upon others beside himself.
It exemplifies the spirit of co-operation and co-ordination in which
only can there be power.
